overview: Respiratory education should connect three scales: gross anatomy and airway protection; physical principles governing breathing; and cellular/molecular gas transport and blood pH. general-overview.label: General Overview
general-overview.style: Accessible and genuinely short, same register as Digestive: short introduction, eight concept-focused sections, bold terms only where useful, no exhaustive anatomy lists unless central.
general-overview.introConcept: Breathing is not simply moving air: it is the first part of a coordinated exchange between the environment, airways, lungs, blood, brain, and metabolically active tissues.

sections.title: Why Breathing Matters
sections.purpose: Begin with cellular demand for O2 and the need to eliminate metabolic CO2; distinguish breathing from cellular respiration; why the system also matters for pH.

sections.title: Alveoli: Where Blood Meets Air
sections.purpose: Branching small airways, extremely thin diffusion surfaces, pulmonary capillaries, Type I/II cells, macrophages and surfactant.

sections.title: How the Chest Moves Air

sections.title: How Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Travel

deep-dive.style: Mechanism-rich, comprehensive, scientifically careful, explicitly differentiated instructor terms and further clarification. Like Digestive Deep Dive, dense enough as serious reference but with clear subheadings and logical teaching sequence.
deep-dive.introConcept: Cover the Chapter 23 study guide completely while adding identification targets from the respiratory anatomy slide deck and carefully distinguishing simplified lecture diagrams from physiological mechanisms.

how-it-connects.label: How It Connects
how-it-connects.style: Narrative first principles from atmospheric oxygen demand to cellular respiration and removal of CO2; one continuous physiologic story, not encyclopedia fragments. Same register as Digestive “Journey of Digestion”.
how-it-connects.workingTitle: From a Breath to a Working Cell — and Back Again
how-it-connects.introConcept: Follow one ordinary breath, including airway conditioning, mechanical inhalation, alveolar diffusion, hemoglobin, tissues, bicarbonate and the brain feedback that drives the next breath.

who-cares.label: Who Cares?
who-cares.targetWords: Three compelling hooks (60–110 words each) with a roughly 350–550-word expandable “More Info” explanation each.
who-cares.style: Digestive/Lymphoid-style surprising title, concrete hook, precise physiological mechanism, strong distinctions and limitations; no sensational health claims.

stories.title: Your lungs need a molecular anti-collapse coating every time you breathe.
stories.hook: Each alveolus is lined with a thin liquid layer whose surface tension tends to pull the air space inward. Type II pneumocytes release surfactant, reducing that tendency and making inflation far easier. It is why a liquid-lined microscopic sac can reliably reopen breath after breath.
moreInfoConcepts: Pulmonary surfactant as lipid/protein mixture (primarily phospholipids)
Type II pneumocytes, mechanics of compliance, lower work of breathing
Premature neonatal respiratory distress as a carefully labeled scientific extension
stories.sourceStatus: Surfactant and alveolar structure directly grounded in lecture; neonatal clinical extension is outside the slides.

stories.title: Your brain often cares more about carbon dioxide than oxygen when deciding to breathe.
stories.hook: At ordinary sea-level conditions, much of the moment-to-moment adjustment of breathing is driven by CO2-linked changes in acidity, not by waiting for oxygen to become dangerously low. The brain monitors the chemistry of the blood and cerebrospinal fluid to adjust how quickly CO2 leaves the lungs.
moreInfoConcepts: Peripheral chemoreceptor response to severe hypoxemia and its limits
stories.sourceStatus: CO2/pH feedback is taught in lecture; modern physiology and relative sensitivity require explicit contextual explanation.

stories.title: Your blood can release more oxygen precisely where tissue chemistry changes.
stories.hook: Hemoglobin does not merely carry oxygen like cargo in a sealed container. Its tendency to hold oxygen changes with surrounding conditions. In actively metabolizing tissues, rising CO2 and acidity can favor oxygen release—a chemical relationship often called the Bohr effect.
moreInfoConcepts: Cooperative oxygen binding and the saturation curve
Higher pO2 promotes loading in lungs
Local H+/CO2 changes favor unloading, tissue context
A conceptual comparison with a dynamically adjusted delivery system, carefully avoiding intentional anthropomorphism
stories.sourceStatus: Curve and pH-related unloading grounded in slides; Bohr-effect name adds explanatory scientific context.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: CO2 is not carried predominantly as carbonic acid
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slide says “Carbonic Acid (H2CO3) – 70%”, but most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate (HCO3−) formed after H2CO3 dissociates. Preserve the lecturer’s ~70/23/7 proportions as approximate but label the chemistry correctly.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Explain carbonic anhydrase catalysis, H2CO3 as transient intermediate, HCO3− in plasma and chloride shift. Do not teach “70% carbonic acid” as literal final form.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slide calls CO2-bound blood blue; actual venous blood remains red (usually darker). Blue in diagrams is a convention.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Retain oxyhemoglobin/carbaminohemoglobin vocabulary, but explicitly correct blue-blood misconception.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: The term external respiration is defined broadly in the lecture
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Lecture labels ventilation, pulmonary gas exchange and transport together as “external respiration”, while many texts reserve external respiration for pulmonary capillary gas exchange.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Teach the three steps exactly as a course framework, then state textbook usage differs.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Nasal nitric oxide and breathing benefits may be overstated
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slides attribute better diffusion and oxygen uptake to nasal breathing/NO without conditions or quantitative support; not all are established as simple universal benefits.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Lead with grounded warming/humidification/filtration/olfaction; describe NO as possible physiological influence, not a guaranteed major boost to oxygen uptake.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Airway histology varies within broad regions
scientificReviewQueue.issue: The whole pharynx is not uniformly stratified squamous; nasopharynx commonly has respiratory mucosa, and nasal vestibule has squamous epithelium. Bronchioles transition in lining.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Keep lecture shortcut for memorization with a short anatomical exception note.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Epiglottis does not provide the only airway protection
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Swallowing-related laryngeal elevation, aryepiglottic structures and true/false fold closure all participate; epiglottis is not a lone mechanical door.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Explain multiple coordinated protections without belaboring it in Exam Cram.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: A rise or fall of one mmHg is an illustrative example
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Atmospheric 760 and alveolar 759/761 mmHg depict an idealized near-sea-level situation, not fixed universal respiratory pressures.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: State the pressure difference and direction matter; absolute atmospheric pressure varies with elevation.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Boyle law needs constant temperature and amount of gas assumptions
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slide presents P=1/V without proportionality constant or assumptions.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Use P∝1/V, or P1V1=P2V2 at constant gas amount and temperature; distinguish the lung’s open airflow from simplified closed gas model.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Apneustic/pneumotaxic centers are useful exam labels but modern control circuitry is distributed; pre-Bötzinger and pontine respiratory groups matter.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Preserve DRG/VRG, apneustic, pneumotaxic exam associations; label modern framework as further scientific context.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Quiet and forced breathing classifications are simplified
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slides equate forced breathing with hyperpnea and VRG as active only in forced breathing. Hyperpnea is increased ventilation, which is not exactly the same as active expiration; VRG includes rhythm-generating networks.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Follow course language for exam while clarifying broader physiology in Deep Dive.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Bronchoconstriction/bronchodilation is more complex than a single nerve pathway
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Simplified sympathetic-versus-parasympathetic language is valid instructional shorthand; bronchial smooth muscle also responds to circulating epinephrine, local mediators and inflammation.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Retain receptor-level autonomic overview, clearly mark immune/local mediators as extension.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Residual volume and direct spirometric measurement
scientificReviewQueue.issue: RV remains after maximal expiration and ordinary spirometry cannot directly obtain it; VC and TLC should be expressed as combinations of basic volumes.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Make a concise table and equation set in the Deep Dive; course slides alone do not teach measurement methods in detail.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Carbaminohemoglobin describes CO2 binding to hemoglobin, but not the primary transport form of CO2. Oxygen unloads in tissues in response to pO2 and also pH/CO2-dependent affinity.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Avoid implying hemoglobin binds O2 and CO2 competitively at exactly the same group; include Bohr-effect caveat.

scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slide uses “apoxia”; “anoxia” is more commonly used for severe/absent oxygen supply. Instructor may expect slide terminology.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Present the original term as used in lecture, note conventional anoxia terminology without silently changing source.

scientificReviewQueue.topic: Nasal vs lung exposure benefits and respiratory portion boundary
scientificReviewQueue.issue: Slides define respiratory portion as “smallest bronchioles & alveoli,” but the shift begins at respiratory bronchioles; terminal bronchioles conduct air.
scientificReviewQueue.handling: Distinguish terminal bronchioles (conducting) from respiratory bronchioles (some exchange) and alveolar ducts/sacs.

studyToolPlanning.note: Stage 4 only. No actual glossary, quiz, fill-in or flashcard records are authored in Stage 1. Questions should be sourced from completed Chapter 23 readings, not generated by Codex.
studyToolPlanning.plannedApproach: Shared concept bank + reviewed practice bank; use stable IDs and link to deep dive/exam cram sections, with explanations of mechanism and realistic distractors.

authoringRules: Match existing Digestive structure, tone and JSON conventions: brief overview, exhaustive Deep Dive, continuous How It Connects, three rich Who Cares? entries, instructor-aligned Exam Cram.
Every study guide question SG-01–SG-29 and terminology list SG-00 must have a direct answer in Exam Cram at Stage 3, not merely an indirect mention.
Preserve slide-language for examination while marking known lecture simplifications in Deep Dive and scientific-review notes; never silently turn misleading shorthand into an authoritative claim.
Use physiology slide references for mechanisms and anatomy slide references for identification targets; no invented citations or model IDs.
Give the General Overview a genuinely introductory reading level, not a miniature Deep Dive; avoid heavy tables in the introduction.
Do not make How It Connects a glossary in prose; follow a real breath and its CO2 return as one chronological physiological process.
“Who Cares?” must remain mechanism-first and precise; short hooks followed by expandable More Info, with distinctions between lecture facts and contextual extensions.
Study Tools are derived from finished educational content and scientific validation, not from mechanically extracting each bold term.
The gallery should select complementary visual figures and preserve source-slide and image-credit metadata; avoid repeated illustration variants.
Do not change the user-provided PowerPoints or study guide, and do not include full proprietary slides in the curriculum blueprint archive.
externalScientificVerification: Not included in Stage 1. Review flags are editorial analysis based on textbook physiology and lecture comparisons; any external research in later stages should be separately cited and labelled.
